It keeps close to the wording of the original and uses the established English of Anglo-Latin legal, liturgical and canon-law formulae. It is an aid to reading the original, not a published translation. div.head: ECf 11.1 B 1
div.ab: ‘Petistis a nobis leges Romanas et Cesaris uobis transmitti, quibus in regno Britannie uti uoluistis. Leges Romanas et Cesaris semper reprobare possumus, legem Dei nequaquam.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 636 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints in smaller type across the page, under ECf retr. 11, 1, and numbers 11, 1 A ff. The dictionary cites it as “ECf 11, 1 A …”, so it is kept with ECf here.

note.seg: vielleicht zielt diese Ablehnung des Römerrechts wieder gegen Absolutisten (s. o. S. 635i); sie hängt aber auch mit dem Englischen Imperialismus zusammen, hier und sonst im 13. Jh.; vgl. Freeman Hist. essays 68; meine Leges Angl. S. 42

perhaps this rejection of Roman law is again aimed at absolutists (see above, p. 635, note i); but it is also connected with English imperialism, here and elsewhere in the 13th century; cf. Freeman, Hist. essays 68; my Leges Angl. p. 42

div.ab: ‘You have asked us that the Roman laws and those of Caesar be sent to you, which you wished to use in the kingdom of Britain. The Roman laws and those of Caesar we can always reject, the law of God never.
